The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, with operator spectrum $\sigma(T)$
([[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then:

1. there is a unique regular projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
   $\sigma$-algebra of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb C$
   such that $\int z\,dE(z)=T$ and, equivalently,
   $$\Phi_E(f)=f(T)\qquad\text{for every continuous }f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C,$$
   where $f(T)$ is the continuous functional calculus of
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]] and
   $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel integral of the projection valued measure $E$;
   this $E$ is the **spectral projection valued measure** of $T$;
2. conversely, if $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb C$ is nonempty and compact and $E$ is
   a regular projection valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of
   $\Lambda$, then $T_E:=\int z\,dE(z)=\Phi_E(z)$ is a bounded normal operator
   with $\sigma(T_E)\subseteq\Lambda$ and $\|T_E\|\le\max_{z\in\Lambda}|z|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and for a bounded measurable $f$ write $\Phi_E(f)=\int f\,dE$ for
the operator of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. Then:

1. $\Phi_E$ is linear and unital: $\Phi_E(\mathbf 1_X)=I$ and
   $\Phi_E(af+bg)=a\Phi_E(f)+b\Phi_E(g)$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ and
   $a,b\in\mathbb C$;
2. $\Phi_E$ is multiplicative: $\Phi_E(fg)=\Phi_E(f)\Phi_E(g)$;
3. $\Phi_E$ preserves conjugation: $\Phi_E(\overline f)=\Phi_E(f)^*$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are bounded measurable with $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, $f$
   is bounded measurable, and $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere,
   meaning $E_x$-almost everywhere for every $x\in H$, then
   $\Phi_E(f_n)\to\Phi_E(f)$ in the strong operator topology.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: For $u\in D(A)$, [F5] and nonnegativity give $\|(I+A)u\|\,\|u\|\ge|\langle(I+A)u,u\rangle|=\|u\|^2+\langle Au,u\rangle\ge\|u\|^2$. Hence $I+A$ is injective and bounded below by $1$. To prove $A$ is closed, suppose $u_n\in D(A)$, $u_n\to u$, and $Au_n\to v$. For every $w\in D(A)$, self-adjointness gives $\langle Aw,u\rangle=\lim_n\langle Aw,u_n\rangle=\lim_n\langle w,Au_n\rangle=\langle w,v\rangle$; by the defining criterion for the adjoint, $u\in D(A^*)$ and $A^*u=v$. Self-adjointness, including equality of domains, yields $u\in D(A)$ and $Au=v$. Thus $A$ is closed. For $w\in D((I+A)^*)$, subtracting the identity term from the defining adjoint relation gives $w\in D(A^*)$ and $(I+A)^*w=w+A^*w$. Conversely, if $w\in D(A^*)$, then $\langle(I+A)u,w\rangle=\langle u,w+A^*w\rangle$ for every $u\in D(A)$, so $w\in D((I+A)^*)$ with $(I+A)^*w=w+A^*w$. Thus $(I+A)^*=I+A^*=I+A$ with domain $D(A)$, so $I+A$ is self-adjoint. If $u_n\in D(A)$ and $(I+A)u_n$ converges, the lower bound makes $(u_n)$ Cauchy; closedness then puts the limit in the range, so the range of $I+A$ is closed. A vector orthogonal to that range lies in $\ker(I+A)^*=\ker(I+A)$, which is zero by the same lower bound; the range is therefore dense and hence all of $H$. Thus $B=(I+A)^{-1}$ exists everywhere, is bounded with norm at most $1$, is injective, and has range $D(A)$, which is dense.

If $x=(I+A)u$ and $y=(I+A)v$, then $\langle Bx,y\rangle=\langle u,(I+A)v\rangle=\langle(I+A)u,v\rangle=\langle x,By\rangle$, so $B$ is self-adjoint. Also $\langle Bx,x\rangle=\langle u,(I+A)u\rangle=\|u\|^2+\langle Au,u\rangle\ge0$, so $B$ is positive. For nonreal $z$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] and self-adjointness give $\|(B-zI)w\|\ge|\operatorname{Im}z|\,\|w\|$ and the same lower bound for its adjoint, so its range is closed and dense. For real $z<0$, positivity and [F5] give $\|(B-zI)w\|\ge(-z)\|w\|$, again giving closed and dense range. For real $z>1$, the Neumann series $(zI-B)^{-1}=z^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}(B/z)^n$ converges in operator norm, so $B-zI$ is invertible as well. Hence $\sigma(B)\subseteq[0,1]$.

By [A1] and [F1], $B$ has its regular spectral PVM $E_B$ on $\sigma(B)$. If $x=E_B(\{0\})y$, then [F4] gives $Bx=\Phi_{E_B}(b\mathbf1_{\{0\}})y=0$, so $E_B(\{0\})H\subseteq\ker B$. Conversely, if $Bx=0$, [F3] gives $0=\|Bx\|^2=\int b^2\,dE_x(b)$. Since $\{b>0\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[1/n,1]$ and $b^2\ge n^{-2}$ on each such interval, $E_x([1/n,1])=0$ for every $n$. Strong countable additivity and $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$ then imply $x=E_B(\{0\})x$. Since $B$ is injective, $E_B(\{0\})=0$. This is a zero spectral projection; it does not remove $0$ from the operator spectrum.

The map $\phi(b)=b^{-1}-1$ on $\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}$ is Borel. For a Borel set $S\subseteq[0,\infty)$ set $E_A(S):=E_B(\{b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}:\phi(b)\in S\})$. Inverse images preserve disjoint unions and intersections, so [F2] makes $E_A$ a PVM; its total value is $E_B(\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\})=I$ because $E_B(\{0\})=0$. The defining identity on indicator functions, extended first to simple functions and then by uniform approximation, gives $\Phi_{E_A}(f)=\Phi_{E_B}(g)$ for every bounded Borel $f$ on $[0,\infty)$, where $g(b)=f(\phi(b))$ for $b>0$ and $g(0)=0$.

Write $\mu_x^B(S)=\langle E_B(S)x,x\rangle$. From the definition in step 4.1, $\mu_x(S)=\mu_x^B(\{b>0:\phi(b)\in S\})$, so $\int\lambda^2\,d\mu_x(\lambda)=\int\phi(b)^2\,d\mu_x^B(b)$. If $x=By$, multiplicativity and the star-homomorphism identity [F4] give $d\mu_x^B(b)=b^2d\mu_y^B(b)$; hence $\int\phi(b)^2\,d\mu_x^B(b)=\int_{(0,1]}(1-b)^2\,d\mu_y^B(b)\le\|y\|^2$. Thus $x$ lies in the domain defining $T_A$. Conversely, if $\int\phi^2\,d\mu_x^B<\infty$, then $\int_{(0,1]}b^{-2}\,d\mu_x^B=\int(\phi+1)^2\,d\mu_x^B\le2\int\phi^2\,d\mu_x^B+2\|x\|^2<\infty$. The bounded truncations $y_N:=\Phi_{E_B}(b^{-1}\mathbf1_{[1/N,1]})(x)$ are Cauchy by the quadratic identity [F3], since their squared tails are tails of this finite integral, and converge to some $y\in H$. Multiplying by $B$ gives $By_N=E_B([1/N,1])x\to x$ by strong countable additivity and $E_B(\{0\})=0$, so $By=x$. Hence $D(T_A)=\operatorname{Ran}B=D(A)$. For $x=By$, the truncation in the definition of $T_A$ is, by step 4.1, $\Phi_{E_B}((1-b)\mathbf1_{[1/(N+1),1]})(y)$. These bounded multipliers converge pointwise off $\{0\}$ to $1-b$ and are uniformly bounded by $1$; [F4] gives strong convergence to $\Phi_{E_B}(1-b)y=(I-B)y=y-x=Ax$. Thus $T_A=A$ on the common domain, proving the operator identity.

If $f$ is bounded Borel on $[0,\infty)$, step 4.1 gives $f(A)=\Phi_{E_B}(g)$ for $g(b)=f(\phi(b))$ on $b>0$ and $g(0)=0$. By [F3], $\|f(A)\|\le\|g\|_\infty\le\sup_{\lambda\ge0}|f(\lambda)|$, and $\|f(A)u\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu_u$. This proves the bounded Borel calculus claims.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. $$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ be the space of smooth complex-valued functions $f$ for which $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|<\infty$ for every pair of multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^2$. Let $(h_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^2}$ be the product Hermite basis of $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ obtained from the multidimensional oscillator at $\hbar=1$, $m_1=m_2=1/2$, and $\omega_1=\omega_2=2$, and write $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\alpha_2$. For $H=-\partial_{x_1}^2-\partial_{x_2}^2+|x|^2$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every integer $r\ge0$ and every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ satisfy

$$\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^2}(1+|\alpha|)^{2r}|\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle_{L^2}|^2\le\|H^r f\|_{L^2}^2<\infty.$$

Consequently the map $f\mapsto(\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle)_\alpha$ is continuous from Schwartz space to each weighted square-summable sequence space with norm $\bigl(\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^{2r}|c_\alpha|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume countable choice. For $f,g\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$,
$$\int\widehat f(\xi)\overline{\widehat g(\xi)}\,d\xi=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx.$$
The pairing is complex-linear in the first variable. In particular $\|\widehat f\|_2=\|f\|_2$.

derivations.claim: Let $I=\mathbb N_0^2$, enumerated by total degree and lexicographic order. For each finite $F\subset I$, let $\mu_F$ have density $\prod_{\alpha\in F}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x_\alpha^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R^F$. [F5] makes these probability laws; integrating out coordinates with [F6] proves their consistency. Each coordinate space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is standard Borel by [F4]. Applying [F1] with [A1] yields $\Omega=\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder $\sigma$-algebra and a probability $\mathbb P$ having these finite marginals. The coordinate variables $\xi_\alpha(\omega)=\omega_\alpha$ are therefore independent standard normals.

For $p\in\mathbb R^2$ put $w_m(p)=(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1/2}$. Since $m>0$, $w_m$ is smooth, and every derivative is bounded: its derivatives are finite sums of polynomial factors divided by positive powers of $|p|^2+m^2$, bounded near the origin and decaying at infinity. The product rule therefore shows multiplication by $w_m$ maps Schwartz space continuously to itself. Define $T_mf=\mathcal F_{2\pi}^{-1}\bigl(w_m(2\pi\cdot)\mathcal F_{2\pi}f\bigr)$. By [F8], $T_mf$ is Schwartz; because $w_m$ is real and even, $T_mf$ is real for real $f$. Under the exact convention in the Statement, $\widehat f(p)=\mathcal F_{2\pi}f(p/(2\pi))$, and the change of variables $p=2\pi\xi$ gives $\widehat{T_mf}(p)=w_m(p)\widehat f(p)$.

For a finite initial segment $I_N$ of the fixed enumeration set $S_N=\sum_{\alpha\in I_N}(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\xi_\alpha^2$. The density in [F5] is normalized, and integration by parts using $(-xe^{-x^2/2})'=(x^2-1)e^{-x^2/2}$ gives $\mathbb E\xi_\alpha^2=1$. Hence $\mathbb E S_N=\sum_{\alpha\in I_N}(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\le\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)(n+1)^{-4}=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-3}=:C<\infty$: grouping $n+1$ in dyadic blocks $[2^j,2^{j+1})$ bounds each block by $2^j2^{-3j}=2^{-2j}$, a summable geometric series. Markov's inequality, which follows from $\mathbf1_{\{S_N>M\}}\le S_N/M$, gives $\mathbb P(S_N>M)\le C/M$. Since the events increase to $\{S:=\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\xi_\alpha^2>M\}$, countable additivity gives $\mathbb P(S>M)\le C/M$; letting integer $M\to\infty$ shows $S<\infty$ on a common event $\Omega_0$ of probability one.

For $f\in\mathcal S_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ put $c_\alpha(f)=\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle$. On $\Omega_0$, [F11] and [F3] give $\sum_\alpha|\xi_\alpha c_\alpha(f)|\le S^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^4|c_\alpha(f)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty$. Thus $W_0(f):=\sum_\alpha\xi_\alpha c_\alpha(f)$ converges absolutely for every $f$ on the same event, is real-linear, and satisfies $|W_0(f)|\le S^{1/2}\|H^2f\|_2$. The last quantity is a continuous Schwartz seminorm by [F3], so each sample is a tempered distribution. Set $W_0=0$ outside $\Omega_0$. Every evaluation $W_0(f)$ is measurable as the almost-sure limit of measurable finite sums, hence $W_0$ is measurable for the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra.

The partial sums for $W_0(f)$ converge in $L^2(\Omega,\mathbb P)$ as well: independence, unit variance, and Parseval in [F10] make their squared $L^2$ tail equal to the corresponding tail of $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha(f)|^2=\|f\|_2^2$. For any finite real combination $\sum_j t_jW_0(f_j)$, a finite partial sum is a linear combination of independent standard normals, with characteristic function $\prod_\alpha e^{-t^2c_\alpha^2/2}=e^{-t^2\sum_\alpha c_\alpha^2/2}$; by [F10] its variance converges to $\|\sum_jt_jf_j\|_2^2$. If $X_N\to X$ in $L^2$, then $|\mathbb E e^{itX_N}-\mathbb E e^{itX}|\le|t|\,\mathbb E|X_N-X|\le|t|\|X_N-X\|_2\to0$, so the limit has the centered normal characteristic function with that variance. Hence the family is jointly Gaussian, centered, and $\mathbb E[W_0(f)W_0(g)]=\int f(x)g(x)\,d^2x$.

Thus $\Phi$ is a measurable $\mathcal S'_\mathbb R$-valued random variable for the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra. From step 4.1 its covariance is $\mathbb E[\Phi(f)\Phi(g)]=\int T_mf(x)T_mg(x)\,d^2x$. Since $f,g$ are real, $\widehat f(-p)=\overline{\widehat f(p)}$ and $\widehat g(-p)=\overline{\widehat g(p)}$; the substitution $p\mapsto-p$ changes this to $(2\pi)^{-2}\int\overline{\widehat f(p)}\widehat g(p)w_m(p)^2\,d^2p=C_m(f,g)$ by step 1.2. The finite-dimensional distributions remain centered Gaussian by step 4.1 and linearity of $T_m$.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.
The Euclidean inclusion of $S^n$ induces its round metric. In spherical coordinates on $S^2$, $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

Let $n\ge1$. For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, its **support** is
$$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\ne0\}}.$$
The function is **compactly supported** if $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact.

A compactly supported $f$ is **compactly supported Riemann integrable** if there is a nondegenerate closed rectangle $Q$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$ such that $f|_Q$ is Riemann integrable. Its integral over Euclidean space is defined by
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f:=\int_Qf.$$
The value is independent of $Q$ by [[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]]. When the support is empty, $f=0$ and the value is $0$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
 $C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb R$ is continuous and compactly

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first variable, and let $A:D(A)\subseteq H\to H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint, and nonnegative, meaning $\langle Au,u\rangle\ge0$ for every $u\in D(A)$. Here self-adjoint means equality with the Hilbert-space adjoint, including equality of domains. A projection-valued measure (PVM) on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ is a map $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(H)$ such that every $E(S)$ is a bounded orthogonal projection ($E(S)^2=E(S)=E(S)^*$), $E(\varnothing)=0$, $E(X)=I$, $E(S\cap T)=E(S)E(T)$, and $E(\bigcup_n S_n)u=\sum_nE(S_n)u$ in norm for each disjoint sequence $(S_n)$ and each $u\in H$. On a locally compact Hausdorff Borel space, such a PVM is regular when each finite scalar measure $\mu_u(S):=\langle E(S)u,u\rangle$ is inner regular on Borel sets and outer regular by open supersets. Then $I+A:D(A)\to H$ is bijective. Its inverse $B:=(I+A)^{-1}$ is a bounded positive (meaning $\langle Bx,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x\in H$) self-adjoint injection with $\|B\|\le1$ and dense range $D(A)$. For a bounded operator, its spectrum $\sigma(B)$ is the set of complex $z$ for which $B-zI$ has no bounded two-sided inverse. Let $E_B$ be the regular spectral PVM on the Borel subsets of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(B)$ satisfying $B=\int_{\sigma(B)}b\,dE_B(b)$. Then $\sigma(B)\subseteq[0,1]$ and $E_B(\{0\})=0$. Define $\phi(b)=b^{-1}-1$ for $b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}$ and, for every Borel $S\subseteq[0,\infty)$, define

$$E_A(S):=E_B(\{b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}:\phi(b)\in S\}).$$

This is a PVM on the Borel subsets of $[0,\infty)$. For each $u\in H$ put $\mu_u(S):=\langle E_A(S)u,u\rangle$. The unbounded integral $\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)$ denotes the operator $T_A$ with domain

$$D(T_A):=\left\{u\in H:\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda^2\,d\mu_u(\lambda)<\infty\right\}$$

and action

$$T_Au:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Phi_{E_A}(\lambda\mathbf1_{[0,N]})(u),$$

where $\Phi_{E_A}(g)$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral of $g$. Then $A=T_A$ and hence

$$A=\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda),\qquad D(A)=\left\{u\in H:\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda^2\,d\langle E_A(\lambda)u,u\rangle<\infty\right\}.$$

For every bounded Borel function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, $f(A):=\Phi_{E_A}(f)$ is bounded, satisfies $\|f(A)\|\le\sup_{\lambda\ge0}|f(\lambda)|$, and obeys $\|f(A)u\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu_u$. The condition $E_B(\{0\})=0$ does not assert that $0\notin\sigma(B)$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: On $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with standard basis $(e_n)_{n\ge1}$ define $D(A)=\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2|x_n|^2<\infty\}$ and $(Ax)_n=nx_n$. Finite sequences lie in $D(A)$ and are dense. For $x\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F2] gives $\sum n|x_n|^2\le(\sum n^2|x_n|^2)^{1/2}(\sum|x_n|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$, so $\langle Ax,x\rangle=\sum n|x_n|^2\ge0$ and $A$ is nonnegative.

The operator is self-adjoint. If $y\in D(A^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2$ with $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every finite sequence $x$; choosing $x=e_n$ gives $z_n=ny_n$, so $\sum n^2|y_n|^2=\|z\|^2<\infty$ and $y\in D(A)$. Conversely, if $y\in D(A)$ then $z=(ny_n)\in\ell^2$ satisfies the adjoint identity for every $x\in D(A)$: both inner-product series converge by [F2] because $Ax,y,x,z\in\ell^2$, and their terms agree. Thus $D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $A^*=A$.

The inverse of $I+A$ is the bounded diagonal operator $B e_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$. Indeed for any $x\in\ell^2$, $y_n=x_n/(n+1)$ satisfies $\sum n^2|y_n|^2\le\sum|x_n|^2$, and $(I+A)y=x$. The operator $B$ is positive and injective, but it is not bounded below because $\|Be_n\|=(n+1)^{-1}\to0$ for unit vectors $e_n$. The vector $y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}$ belongs to $\ell^2$: for $n\ge2$, $n^{-2}\le(n-1)^{-1}-n^{-1}$, so $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}\le2$. It is not in $\operatorname{Ran}B$, since $Bx=y$ would require $x_n=(n+1)/n>1$ for every $n$, which is not square-summable. Hence $B$ is not surjective and $0\in\sigma(B)$.

Define $E_B(S)x=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}x_ne_n$ for Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$. Its values are orthogonal coordinate projections, and the coordinate definition gives $E_B(\varnothing)=0$, $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$, and $E_B(S)E_B(T)=E_B(S\cap T)$. For disjoint Borel $S_k$, each coordinate $n$ occurs in at most one projection, so the partial sums $\sum_{k\le N}E_B(S_k)x$ converge in $\ell^2$ to $E_B(\bigcup_kS_k)x$: the squared norm of the omitted coordinates is a tail of the convergent nonnegative series $\sum_n|x_n|^2$. Thus $E_B$ is strongly countably additive. It integrates the coordinate function to $B$, because its integral acts diagonally by $(n+1)^{-1}$ on each $e_n$. For every $x$, its finite scalar measure is $\mu_x(S):=\langle E_B(S)x,x\rangle=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}|x_n|^2$. For any Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$, the finite set $K_N:=\{(n+1)^{-1}:n\le N,\ (n+1)^{-1}\in S\}$ is compact and contained in $S$, and $\mu_x(K_N)\uparrow\mu_x(S)$ because $\sum_n|x_n|^2<\infty$. Hence $\mu_x$ is inner regular on every Borel set. Since $\sigma(B)$ is compact, for any Borel $S$ and $\varepsilon>0$, inner regularity of $S^c$ gives a compact $K\subseteq S^c$ with $\mu_x(S^c\setminus K)<\varepsilon$; then the open set $\sigma(B)\setminus K$ contains $S$ and its excess measure is less than $\varepsilon$. Thus $\mu_x$ is also outer regular, so $E_B$ is a regular PVM. Hence [F1] identifies it with the bounded-resolvent spectral PVM. Since no atom is at zero, $E_B(\{0\})=0$, although step 3.1 proves $0\in\sigma(B)$. This refutes the asserted implication and shows why a zero spectral projection must be distinguished from a spectral value.
